title: Russian Empire
wiki_lead:
The Russian Empire was the final phase of the Russian monarchy. It spanned most of northern Eurasia from its establishment in 1721 until the proclamation of the Russian Republic in 1917. At its height in the late 19th century, it covered approximately 22,800,000 km2 (8,800,000 sq mi), roughly one-sixth of the world's landmass, making it the third-largest empire in history, after the British and Mongol empires.
The foundations of the empire were laid by Ivan III (r. 1462–1505), who established a centralized Russian state. His grandson, Ivan IV (r. 1533–1584), was the first Russian monarch to be crowned tsar in 1547. Between 1550 and 1700, Russia grew by an average of 35,000 km2 (14,000 sq mi) per year. Peter the Great (r. 1682–1725) transformed the tsardom into an empire and fought wars that turned Russia into a major European power. He moved the capital from Moscow to the newly established city of Saint Petersburg, initiated political reforms, and led a cultural revolution. Catherine the Great (r. 1762–1796) presided over further Russian expansion while continuing Peter's policy of modernization. Alexander I (r. 1801–1825) helped defeat Napoleon during the Napoleonic Wars and established the Holy Alliance, which aimed to restrain the spread of secularism and liberalism across Europe. Although Russia had achieved victories in the Russo-Turkish wars, its defeat in the Crimean War (1853–1856) prompted a period of domestic reform and redirected its expansion toward Central Asia. Alexander II (r. 1855–1881) initiated major reforms, most notably the 1861 emancipation of approximately 23 million serfs. The 19th century also saw major developments in literature, music, and the sciences.
By the start of the 19th century, Russian territory extended from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the Black Sea in the south, and from the Baltic Sea in the west to the Pacific Ocean and Alaska in the east. Russia administered Alaska between 1799 and 1867. Russia also expanded its control over the Caucasus, most of Central Asia, and parts of Northeast Asia. By the 1897 census, the population had reached 126 million, with vast ethnic, linguistic, and socioeconomic diversity. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Russia experienced industrial growth and railway construction, though the country remained largely agrarian. Famine, political discontent, and resistance to reform contributed to growing unrest and the rise of revolutionary movements. Following the 1905 Revolution, Nicholas II (r. 1894–1917) authorized the creation of a national parliament, the State Duma, though ultimate political authority remained with him.
Russia entered the First World War in 1914 on the side of the Allies. High casualties, military setbacks, and severe food and fuel shortages in the cities led to widespread discontent with the monarchy. In 1917, mass unrest in Petrograd and army mutinies culminated in the February Revolution, which led to Nicholas II's abdication and the establishment of the Russian Provisional Government. Political instability, continued participation in the unpopular war, and economic disruption resulted in mass demonstrations in July, after which the government proclaimed a republic in September. The Provisional Government was overthrown in the October Revolution by the Bolsheviks. They established a communist state and signed a treaty ending Russia's involvement in the war, but faced opposition from various factions known collectively as the Whites. After emerging victorious in the Russian Civil War, the Bolsheviks established the Soviet Union across most of Russian territory. Russia was one of four continental empires to collapse as a result of World War I, along with Germany, Austria–Hungary, and the Ottoman Empire.

By 1914, its population exceeded 167 million, comprising Russians alongside numerous ethnic minorities including Poles, Ukrainians, Finns, Caucasians, and Central Asians, governed through a centralized bureaucracy under absolute monarchical rule with limited noble and clerical input. The empire's defining characteristics included aggressive territorial aggrandizement, which doubled its size multiple times over two centuries, and reforms aimed at modernization, such as Peter the Great's westernization efforts, Catherine II's enlightenment-inspired legal codes and territorial gains against the Ottoman Empire and Poland, and Alexander II's emancipation of serfs in 1861 that freed approximately 23 million peasants from bondage akin to hereditary slavery. These achievements fostered economic growth, including early industrialization and vast resource extraction, positioning Russia as a major European power capable of defeating Napoleon's invasion in 1812 and influencing global affairs through alliances and conflicts.
